articles.author: Pawel Wolanski
articles.description:
Recently I have been involved in Framework Update engagement to bump Commerce Cloud solution from JDK 17 to JDK 21.
Upgrade to Java 21 It has been announced some time ago by SAP as a Framework Update
SAP Learning

Medium blog post
LinkedIn blog post
One of nice things which has been added by SAP is upgrade automation based on OpenRewrite. More information about whole activity you can find as SAP KBA 3618495 - Using OpenRewrite recipes to support SAP Commerce Cloud JDK21 Framework Update adoption
At the beginning when you run ant command ant gradle you may get similar error like:
/opt/hybris/hybris/bin/platform/build.xml:204: Cannot invoke "String.startsWith(String)" because the return value of "org.apache.maven.model.Dependency.getVersion()" is null

That error is related to scanning process for Maven dependencies in external-dependencies.xml. 
In my case one of external-dependencies.xml for custom extension got dependency defined:
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
    xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
    <groupId>de.hybris.platform</groupId>
    <artifactId>knackbravaocc</artifactId>
    <version>2211.1</version>
    <packaging>jar</packaging>

    <dependencies>
...
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        </dependency>
...
    </dependencies>
</project>

In order to fix it, I needed to add version explicitly for that dependency.
Check if your all dependencies have version xml tag defined.
articles.title: SAP Commerce Cloud Framework Update JDK 21 - issue with ANT gradle target

articles.author: Allan Roberto
articles.description:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are everywhere — but most developers rely heavily on cloud providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, or Azure.
But what if you could run models locally on your machine?
That’s where Ollama comes in.
In this article, I’ll explain:
Why you should consider using Ollama
When it makes sense
The real limitations (especially GPU vs CPU)
Lessons learned from using it in a Spring Boot project
Ollama is a tool that allows you to run LLMs locally with a simple CLI/API.
Example:
ollama run llama3

Or via HTTP:
POST http://localhost:11434/api/generate

It abstracts away:
Model downloads
Runtime configuration
Inference execution
No API calls → no billing → perfect for:
Local testing
Prototyping
Feature validation
Your data never leaves your machine:
Great for sensitive use cases
Useful for regulated environments
You can run LLMs:
Without internet
Without external dependencies
No network latency:
Immediate responses
Easier debugging
This is where most developers get surprised.



Resource
Experience




CPU only
Slow inference (seconds per response)


GPU (8GB+)
Much faster, usable in real apps


High-end GPU
Near real-time performance






Model
RAM Requirement




7B
~4–8 GB


13B
~10–16 GB


70B
🔥 Not for laptops



If you're using:
A basic notebook (8–16GB RAM, no GPU) → expect:


Slow responses
Limited models
Occasional crashes
If you have:
Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3) → surprisingly good performance
NVIDIA GPU → best experience
In your repository, the idea is simple:
Spring Boot → HTTP call → Ollama (localhost) → Model response

This gives you:
Full control over AI behavior
No dependency on external providers during development
✔ Ollama is amazing for development
Ollama is not a replacement for cloud AI — it’s a development superpower.
Use it to:
Experiment fast
Validate ideas
Build locally
But don’t expect production-level performance without serious hardware.
articles.title: Running LLMs Locally with Ollama: Benefits, Limitations, and Hardware Reality

articles.author: Odilon HUGONNOT
articles.description:
ClaudeGate exposes Claude Code CLI as a REST API. Every POST /api/v1/jobs request creates a job that spawns a CLI process — this isn't an HTTP handler that fires a SQL query. It's a child process, RAM, CPU, time. Without protection, an aggressive client can saturate the machine in seconds.
The obvious solution: a per-IP rate limiter. The golang.org/x/time/rate package implements the token bucket algorithm, which is exactly what's needed here. Here's how the integration was done, the decisions made, and what was deliberately left out.
A token bucket holds tokens. Each request consumes one token. Tokens replenish at a constant rate (the RPS). If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected.
golang.org/x/time/rate exposes this cleanly via rate.NewLimiter(limit, burst):
import "golang.org/x/ti…
articles.title: Rate limiter in Go: per-IP token bucket with golang.org/x/time/rate

articles.author: Usama Saleem
articles.description:
State Management & Context Drift in Multi-Step AI Workflows
This is one of the biggest hidden problems in AI automation systems.
Everything works… until it doesn’t.
Here’s what’s actually happening under the hood 👇
LLMs are stateless by design
Every request is independent.
There is no real “memory” unless YOU manage it.
So in multi-step workflows:
  Step 1 generates output

  Step 2 depends on it

  Step 3 modifies it

If state is not structured → context breaks.
Context drift starts silently
Over multiple steps:
Important details get dropped
Irrelevant tokens get added
Meaning starts to shift
Result:
  👉 Output becomes inconsistent

  👉 Agents behave unpredictably

Token limits make it worse
You can’t pass full history forever.
So you:
  Trim context ❌

  Summarize ❌

Both introduce:
  Information loss

  Hallucination risk

No single source of truth
In most AI frameworks:
Some data in prompts
Some in memory
Some in DB
This fragmentation causes:
  Conflicts

  Outdated context

  Logic errors

Multi-agent = exponential complexity
When multiple agents interact:
Each has its own context
Each modifies state differently
Now you get:
  👉 State desync

  👉 Conflicting outputs

What actually works in production:
      Structured state (JSON schemas, not raw text)

      External memory (DB/vector store as source of truth)

      Explicit state passing between steps

      Context compression strategies (not blind trimming)

Workflow checkpoints + validation
AI workflows don’t fail because of models.
They fail because of state mismanagement.
Fix the state → you fix reliability.


  
  
  AI #Automation #LLM #Engineering #SaaS
articles.title: There is no real “memory” unless YOU manage it.

articles.description:
Recently, i added some features to my side project flutter app.
If I release to both platforms at once and some bugs occur, it would be difficult to handle.
I couldn't access the main page. The app was stuck on the splash screen.
At that moment, something came to my mind.
So I replaced it with the sign_in_button package and added it to dependencies in the pubspec.yaml file.
It should have been in dependencies, but I accidentally added it to dev_dependencies.

If Flutter packages are placed in the dev_dependencies section, the app can still build while running in the debug environment.
Otherwise, crash problems can happen.
Google Play Store reviewers are not that strict, i think.
I assume they didn't test my new build in the release environment.
Anyway, I fixed the packages in pubspec.yaml properly.
articles.title: Flutter App Stuck on Splash Screen: A dev_dependencies Mistake
